Object or record generally accepted as payment for goods and services and repayment of debts, such as [[Tax|taxes]], in a particular country or socio-economic context. Its distinguishing functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and, sometimes, standard of deferred payment; most modern textbooks list only the first three.

Money was historically an emergent market phenomenon with intrinsic value as a commodity. Nearly all contemporary systems rest on unbacked fiat money, whose value derives from social convention and a government's declaration of legal tender. The money supply comprises currency in circulation and, depending on the definition, bank money, which forms by far the largest part of broad money in developed countries.

The word derives from Latin *moneta* 'coin', named for the temple of Juno Moneta, site of the Roman mint. Societies used commodity money such as cowry shells; the Mesopotamian shekel was a unit of weight based on about 160 grains of [[Barley|barley]]. According to [[Herodotus]], the Lydians first used gold and silver coins, which modern scholars date to c. 650–600 BC. [[Paper money]] first appeared in China during the [[Song dynasty]] as *jiaozi*, evolving from promissory notes used since the 7th century; [[Marco Polo]] described it under the [[Yuan dynasty]]. Stockholms Banco issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661. By the early 20th century almost all countries had adopted the gold standard. After [[World War II]], most countries fixed fiat currencies to the [[United States dollar|U.S. dollar]], itself fixed to gold until the U.S. government suspended convertibility in 1971.

Largest contiguous empire in history, originating in present-day [[Mongolia]] and at its height stretching from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe, north into Siberia and south into the Indian subcontinent.

The empire emerged from the unification of several nomadic tribes under Temüjin, whom a council proclaimed ruler of all Mongols in 1206 with the title [[Genghis Khan]]. It grew rapidly under him and his descendants, who sent armies in every direction, conquering the Iranian plateau, invading Southeast Asia and reaching the Levant and the Carpathian Mountains. Its mobile cavalry armies were organized on a decimal system of units of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000. The conquests caused widespread depopulation in affected regions, with some estimates of 40 million or more deaths. The resulting *Pax Mongolica* allowed trade, technologies, commodities, and ideologies to move across Eurasia.

Succession disputes split the empire, as Genghis Khan's grandchildren contested whether the line should follow his son Ögedei or other sons such as Tolui, Chagatai, or [[Jochi]]. After Möngke Khan died in 1259, rival councils elected his brothers Ariq Böke and [[Kublai Khan]], who fought the Toluid Civil War (1260–1264). By Kublai's death in 1294 the empire had fractured into four khanates: the [[Golden Horde]], the Chagatai Khanate, the [[Ilkhanate]], and the [[Yuan dynasty]] in China, so named by Kublai in an edict of December 18, 1271.

The Ilkhanate disintegrated between 1335 and 1353. The Yuan lost China in 1368 to Ming forces and retreated north as the Northern Yuan, which survived until conquest by the [[Qing dynasty]] in the 1630s. The Golden Horde's rule in Eastern Europe is traditionally considered to have ended in 1480, and the Chagatai Khanate lasted until 1687.

Earth's only [[Natural satellite|natural satellite]], a differentiated, terrestrial body with a diameter of 3,474 km.

The Moon orbits Earth in an elliptical path, completing an orbit relative to the Earth and Sun every 29.5 days (a lunar month) and relative to the stars every 27.3 days. Gravitational attraction between the two bodies produces tides on Earth and has pulled the Moon into [[Tidal locking|tidal locking]], so that it always shows the same near side to Earth. Libration makes about 59% of the surface visible from Earth.

Its mass is 1.2% that of Earth, and its diameter is roughly one-quarter of Earth's. It is larger and more massive than any known dwarf planet and is the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System, the largest relative to its parent planet. Its surface gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, second-highest among moons after Io. It has only a minuscule hydrosphere, atmosphere, and magnetic field. The surface is covered with regolith dust and marked by impact craters, some with bright rays. The Moon was volcanically active until 1.2 billion years ago; lava filling ancient craters, mostly on the thinner near side, formed the dark basaltic plains called maria ('seas'). The reflectance of its surface is comparable to that of asphalt, yet it is the brightest object in Earth's night sky.

Isotope dating of lunar samples suggests the Moon formed in the first 200 million years after the Solar System's origin. The prevailing theory holds that a giant impact of a Mars-sized body named [[Theia (hypothetical planet)|Theia]] with the proto-Earth ejected material that accreted into the Moon. Its apparent size matches the Sun's, so it covers the Sun completely during a total solar eclipse, and when it passes through Earth's shadow a [[Lunar eclipse|lunar eclipse]] occurs. Its changing illuminated portion produces the lunar phases.

The first spaceflights to another body were to the Moon: Luna 1 flew past in 1959 and Luna 2 struck it, both launched by the [[Soviet Union]]; Luna 9 made the first soft landing in 1966, and Luna 10 the first orbital insertion. Humans first orbited it on Apollo 8 on December 24, 1968, and landed on [[Apollo 11]] on July 20, 1969. By 1972 six Apollo missions had landed twelve people, making the Moon the only celestial body beyond Earth that humans have visited. Plans to return, including the [[Artemis program]] and its Artemis II crewed flyby of 2026, are driven partly by robotic confirmation of water on the Moon.

Standard, doctrine or system of conduct through which communities and individuals evaluate actions, character, and social arrangements; a quality found among social animals, including humans.

The criteria used vary across individuals, societies, social classes, religions, cultures, and traditions, and include rightness or wrongness, virtue or vice, honor or disgrace, reciprocity, and shame. Cross-cultural research suggests that attention to moral sentiments exists in all human societies. Moral universalism holds that some principles, such as honesty, loyalty, and fairness, are recognized by all societies, while moral relativism denies that any universal morality exists. Immorality is the violation of morality; [[Nihilism|nihilism]] rejects morality as a concept, and amorality is variously defined as unawareness of, indifference to, or disbelief in any set of moral standards. Some researchers argue that moral capacities evolved to facilitate cooperation, with precursors visible in non-human primates.

The English word derives from the [[Latin]] *mōs* (genitive *mōris*), 'manner, character, proper behavior', through Late Latin *mōrālitās* and Old French *moralité*. It entered Middle English around 1375 in the works of [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]. The Latin adjective *mōrālis* was coined by [[Cicero]] to translate a Greek term.

[[Ethics]], or moral philosophy, is the branch of philosophy that addresses questions of morality, and the two words are often used interchangeably. Simon Blackburn notes a usage that restricts morality to systems such as that of [[Immanuel Kant]], based on duty, obligation, and principles, and reserves ethics for the Aristotelian approach based on virtue. In its descriptive sense, morality refers to the values and codes of conduct a society is observed to accept; in its normative sense, it refers to whatever is actually right or wrong, which may be independent of those values. Three major approaches in normative ethics are [[Consequentialism|consequentialism]], deontological ethics, and virtue ethics, which differ in whether outcomes, duties, or character have the central role in evaluation.

Country, North Africa, officially the Kingdom of Morocco, with coastlines on the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean.

It borders Algeria to the east and the disputed territory of Western Sahara to the south, and has an area of about 716,550 sq km and a population of approximately 37 million. The capital is [[Rabat]]; the largest city is [[Casablanca]]. Spain holds the exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla on the northern coast, which Morocco claims.

The region has been inhabited since the Paleolithic era, more than 300,000 years ago. The Moroccan state traces its origins to the Idrisid dynasty, established by Idris I in 788. Morocco reached its zenith as a regional power in the 11th and 12th centuries under the Berber [[Almoravid dynasty]] and the Almohads, when it controlled the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the Maghreb. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portugal seized some territory, but Morocco was the only North African nation to escape Ottoman rule. The Saadi Sultanate conquered the [[Songhai Empire]] in the late 16th century. The Alawi dynasty, which still rules, took power in 1631. In 1912 France and Spain established protectorates and designated [[Tangier]] an international zone; Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V.

Morocco is a unitary semi-constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. The king, Mohammed VI since 1999, holds vast executive and legislative powers, especially over the military, foreign policy, and religious affairs. Islam is the official and predominant religion; Arabic and Tamazight are official languages. Morocco has the fifth-largest economy in Africa and belongs to the [[Arab League]] and the [[African Union]]. Phosphates, agriculture, tourism, and automobile manufacturing are leading economic sectors.

The status of [[Western Sahara]] remains unresolved. After Spain agreed in 1975 to leave the territory, a guerrilla war broke out; Mauritania relinquished its claim in 1979, and a ceasefire was reached in 1991. Morocco, which calls the area its Southern Provinces, administers most of it, while the Polisario Front seeks independence.

Capital and most populous city of Russia, on the Moskva River in Central Russia.

The city has more than 13 million residents within its limits, more than 19.1 million in the urban area, and more than 21.5 million in the metropolitan area. It covers 2,511 sq km and is the most populous city entirely in Europe. It is the northernmost and coldest [[Megacity|megacity]] in the world and is governed as a federal city.

Moscow was first documented in 1147. As capital of the [[Grand Principality of Moscow]] it led the unification of Russian lands in the 15th century, and it remained a political and economic center after the [[Tsardom of Russia]] was proclaimed in 1547. [[Peter the Great]] moved the capital to the newly founded [[Saint Petersburg]] in 1712, and Moscow declined in importance until the capital returned in 1918. It then became the political center of the [[Soviet Union]] and grew greatly. After the Soviet dissolution it remained the capital of the Russian Federation.

Moscow is Russia's political, economic, cultural, and scientific center. Its urban economy is among the world's largest, and it has the second-highest number of billionaires of any city, tied with Hong Kong. The Moscow International Business Center features the majority of Europe's tallest skyscrapers. The city hosted the 1980 Summer Olympics and co-hosted the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Its architecture includes Red Square, Saint Basil's Cathedral, and the Moscow [[Kremlin]], seat of the Government of Russia; several sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Bolshoi Theatre and [[Moscow State University]] are among its institutions. Transit includes four international airports, ten railway terminals, a tram system, a monorail, and the Moscow Metro, the busiest metro system in Europe and one of the largest [[Rapid transit|rapid transit]] systems in the world. More than 40% of the city's territory is covered by greenery.

Hebrew prophet in the [[Abrahamic religions]] who led the [[Israelites]] out of slavery in the Exodus from Egypt.

He is considered the most important prophet in Judaism and Samaritanism, and one of the most important in Christianity, Islam, and the Baháʼí Faith. According to the scriptures, God dictated the Mosaic Law to him, and he wrote it down as part of the [[Torah]]; tradition ascribes to him the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.

According to the Book of Exodus, Moses was born while the enslaved Israelites were increasing in number. When Pharaoh ordered all newborn Hebrew boys killed, his mother, Jochebed, hid him in the bulrushes along the [[Nile]], where Pharaoh's daughter found and adopted him, so that he grew up in the Egyptian royal family. After killing an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, he fled to Midian, where the Angel of the Lord spoke to him from a burning bush on Mount Horeb. God sent him back to Egypt to demand the Israelites' release, and his elder brother Aaron spoke for him. After the Ten Plagues, Moses led the Exodus across the Red Sea to Mount Sinai, where he received the [[Ten Commandments]]. After 40 years of wandering in the desert, he died on Mount Nebo at the age of 120, within sight of the Promised Land.

The name may derive from the Egyptian root *msy* ('child of'), as in Thutmose; the Bible gives it a Hebrew folk etymology, 'I drew him out of the water'.

The majority of scholars see the biblical Moses as a legendary figure, while allowing that Moses or a similar figure may have existed in the 13th century BC. No contemporary Egyptian records confirm the events described, though the Merneptah Stele mentions "Israel" in Canaan around 1208 BC. Estimates of his lifespan differ: the authors of *Seder Olam Rabbah* calculated 1391–1271 BC, while [[Jerome]] suggested 1592 BC as his birth year. The Egyptian character of his name was recognized by ancient writers such as Philo and [[Josephus]]. Moses has often been portrayed in art, literature, music, and film.

Change in the position of an object or fluid with respect to a [[Frame of reference|reference frame]] over a given time.

Motion is described mathematically by vector quantities such as displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The branch of physics describing motion without reference to its cause is [[Kinematics|kinematics]]; the branch studying forces and their effect on motion is dynamics. An object not moving relative to a given frame is said to be at rest. Because modern physics holds that there is no absolute frame of reference, [[Isaac Newton]]'s concept of absolute motion cannot be determined, and everything in the universe can be considered to be in motion. The concept applies not only to objects and matter but also to waves, radiation, fields, and space-time. Common types include translational, projectile, circular, rotational, and oscillatory motion.

[[Classical mechanics]] describes macroscopic objects moving much slower than the speed of light, from projectiles and machinery to spacecraft, planets, and stars. It rests on [[Newton's laws of motion]], first compiled in his *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, published on July 5, 1687. The first law states that a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion stays in motion, unless acted on by an external force; the second relates force to the change in momentum, equal to mass times acceleration for constant mass; the third states that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. These laws unified the motion of celestial bodies with that of objects on Earth.

Modern kinematics, developed alongside the study of electromagnetism, refers velocities to the speed of light and transforms them by Lorentz transformations; this is [[Special relativity|special relativity]]. W. K. Clifford and Albert Einstein used differential geometry to incorporate gravity, producing [[General relativity|general relativity]]. At the atomic and subatomic level, [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] applies. Because of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, a particle's location and velocity cannot be determined simultaneously, and matter and radiation show wave–particle duality. Quantum mechanics also helps explain large-scale phenomena such as superfluidity and superconductivity.

Elevated portion of a planet's surface, generally with steep sides showing significant exposed [[Bedrock|bedrock]].

No universally accepted definition exists; elevation, volume, relief, steepness, spacing, and continuity have all been used as criteria. A mountain is usually considered higher than a hill and is often thought of as higher than 2,000 feet (610 m), the threshold the U.K. government uses for access purposes. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names abandoned its 1,000-foot (305 m) definition in the 1970s. A few mountains are isolated summits, but most occur in mountain ranges. By one UN Environment Programme classification, 24% of Earth's land mass is mountainous.

There are three main types of mountains: volcanic, fold, and block. All are formed through [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]], when portions of the crust move, crumple, and dive. Volcanic mountains, such as [[Mount Fuji]] in Japan and [[Mount Pinatubo]] in the Philippines, are built where a plate is pushed below another or at a mid-ocean ridge or hotspot. Fold mountains arise when two plates collide, shortening the crust along thrust faults. Formation acts on time scales of up to tens of millions of years. Once building ceases, mountains are slowly leveled by weathering, mass wasting, and [[Erosion|erosion]] by rivers and glaciers.

High elevations produce colder climates than sea level at similar latitude, so different elevations support different plants and animals. Because of the less hospitable terrain and climate, mountains are used less for agriculture and more for resource extraction, such as mining and logging, and for recreation, such as climbing and skiing.

The highest mountain on Earth above sea level is [[Mount Everest]] in the Himalayas, whose summit is 8,850 m above mean sea level. The highest known mountain on any planet in the Solar System is [[Olympus Mons]] on Mars, at 21,171 m. Measured from base to peak, [[Mauna Kea]] in Hawaii rises 9,330 m from the ocean floor, and some scientists consider it the tallest on Earth.

Early modern empire in South Asia, 1526–1857.

At its peak it stretched from the fringes of the Indus River Basin in the west and northern Afghanistan in the northwest to Kashmir in the north, the highlands of Assam and Bangladesh in the east, and the Deccan Plateau in the south.

It is conventionally said to have been founded in 1526 by [[Babur]], a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley, who defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, at the First Battle of Panipat, shattering a larger army with firearms and cannons. His son [[Humayun]] was driven into exile in Persia by [[Sher Shah Suri]], returned in 1555, and died the next year. [[Akbar]] (r. 1556–1605) consolidated the empire. The imperial structure is sometimes dated from Akbar's rule in 1600 and lasted until 1720, shortly after the death of [[Aurangzeb]] (r. 1658–1707), under whom the empire reached its greatest extent. It was reduced to the area around Old Delhi by 1760, and the British Raj formally dissolved it after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

Though created by warfare, the empire did not vigorously suppress the cultures it ruled, instead governing through new administrative practices and diverse ruling elites. Its wealth rested on agricultural taxes introduced by Akbar, amounting to well over half a peasant cultivator's output and paid in a well-regulated silver currency. Akbar's policy of *sulh-i-kul* ('universal peace') abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims. Critics argue that Aurangzeb's reimposition of the jizya and stricter application of Islamic law alienated non-Muslim subjects and fueled rebellions by Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, and Rajputs. After his death, weak successors, succession wars, and regional powers eroded Mughal control; [[Nader Shah]] attacked Delhi in 1739.

Relative peace in the 17th century aided India's economic expansion, and court wealth patronized painting, literature, textiles, and architecture, especially under [[Shah Jahan]]. Mughal UNESCO World Heritage Sites include Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Lahore Fort, the Shalamar Gardens, and the [[Taj Mahal]].
